title: Elastic vs inelastic collisions
examples: When does kinetic energy stay the same in a collision?
How can I tell if a collision is elastic?
What is the difference between momentum and kinetic energy?

explain.say: Today we look at collisions and energy. We check if kinetic energy is conserved.

items: Kinetic energy is energy of motion.
We check if this energy is conserved.

explain.say: In a perfectly elastic collision, kinetic energy is conserved. This means no energy is lost.
In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is not conserved. Some energy is lost as heat or sound.
A completely inelastic collision involves sticking together after impact. Kinetic energy is definitely lost here.
Consider two billiard balls colliding perfectly. If they bounce apart with the same speed, KE is conserved.
When a car crashes and deforms, kinetic energy is not conserved. The energy turns into heat and sound waves.

faq.q: Is momentum always conserved in any collision?
faq.a: Yes, momentum is always conserved in any collision within a closed system. This is a fundamental law of physics.
asks: Does momentum always stay the same?

faq.q: What is the difference between elastic and inelastic?
faq.a: Elastic means kinetic energy is conserved, while inelastic means some kinetic energy is lost.

faq.q: Can a collision be both elastic and inelastic?
faq.a: No, a collision must be one or the other. If KE is lost, it is inelastic, even if momentum is conserved.
asks: Is there overlap between the types?

faq.q: What is the most perfectly elastic collision?
faq.a: The theoretical perfect elastic collision is rare in the real world. It assumes no energy is lost to heat or sound.
asks: How perfect can an elastic collision be?

faq.q: Does the object sticking together mean KE is lost?
faq.a: Yes, when objects stick together, this is the most inelastic type of collision. Kinetic energy is converted into other forms.
asks: If they stick, what happens to energy?

facts: Momentum is always conserved in any collision.
Kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions.
Inelastic collisions often convert KE into heat or sound.
The most inelastic collision involves objects sticking together.

quiz.say: Two carts collide and bounce apart, and you calculate the initial and final kinetic energies. If they are equal, what type of collision occurred?
quiz.why: Because the initial and final kinetic energies are equal, energy was conserved, which defines an elastic collision.

wrong.1: This is tempting because most real-world collisions lose energy, but the problem states the energies are equal.
wrong.2: This implies the objects stuck together, which is not what the problem describes.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because the conservation of energy is a key indicator for the collision type.

quiz.say: A bowling ball hits a stationary pin, and the pin falls over. If you measure the energy before and after, and find a difference, what must have happened?
quiz.why: The loss of energy suggests that some energy was converted into forms other than motion, making it inelastic.

wrong.1: If KE were conserved, the energy measurements would match perfectly.
wrong.2: Momentum is always conserved, so this option is physically impossible.
wrong.3: This term specifically means KE is conserved, which contradicts the measurement of energy loss.

quiz.say: When two objects collide and stick together, what is the status of kinetic energy?

options.show: KE is converted to potential energy
options.say: KE is converted to potential energy

quiz.why: Sticking together is the most inelastic type of collision, meaning kinetic energy is not conserved.

wrong.0: While potential energy changes, the primary loss mechanism in sticking is usually heat or sound.
wrong.1: This is too general; the specific outcome of sticking together means a definite loss of KE.
wrong.3: This would only happen if the objects bounced apart perfectly.
